Ergodicity.long:
A process is ergodic when the average across many participants equals the average for one participant over time. Most statistics people quote assume this quietly, and trading returns do not satisfy it.

The standard illustration: a bet that pays +50 per cent or loses 40 per cent on a coin flip. Across a thousand people playing once, the average outcome is positive — the ensemble average grows. One person playing a thousand times in a row almost certainly ends near zero, because the multiplication compounds the losses. Same bet, same odds, two completely different answers, and only the second one describes an account.

The practical consequence is that expected value calculated the usual way is the wrong tool for anything you repeat with your own capital. What matters is the time average — what happens to the sequence you personally live through — and that is dragged down by volatility in a way the arithmetic mean never shows.

Where people get fooled: positive expectancy is treated as sufficient. It is not. A strategy with a genuinely positive expected value can still ruin every individual who runs it, if the position sizes are large enough that a bad sequence removes the capital needed to continue. That is not a paradox; it is what non-ergodicity means, and it is the mathematical reason position sizing is not optional.
Ergodicity.usage: Generally invoked to explain why an expected value computed across outcomes says little about the path one account actually takes.

Path dependence.long:
A result is path dependent when the ORDER of the returns changes the outcome, not merely which returns occurred. Multiplication is commutative, so on paper a set of percentage moves compounds to the same figure in any order — which is exactly why the idea gets dismissed too quickly.

The order starts mattering the moment anything else touches the account. Add withdrawals and an early drawdown removes capital that would have compounded later. Add leverage and a bad stretch arriving first can force a liquidation that a bad stretch arriving last would not. Add a human and an early run of losses changes the size they are willing to trade afterwards, which changes everything downstream.

This is the mechanism behind sequence risk in retirement planning and behind why two traders with identical annual returns can end up in very different places.

Where people get fooled: backtests report the final figure and hide the ordering entirely. A curve that ended up is compatible with a drawdown deep enough that no real person would have kept trading through it — and if they stopped, they never reached the ending the backtest reports. Read the worst stretch and where it sits, not only the total.
Path dependence.usage: Typically raised alongside sequence risk: the same returns in a different order produce different outcomes once withdrawals, leverage or human behaviour are involved.

Variance drain.long:
Variance drain is the gap between the arithmetic average of a series of returns and what they actually compound to. The compounded result is always lower, and the gap grows with volatility.

The arithmetic is easy to check. Alternate plus ten per cent and minus ten per cent: the average is zero, and the compounded outcome is a loss of about one per cent for every pair. Widen the swings to plus and minus fifty and the average is still zero while the compounded loss per pair is twenty-five per cent. The average did not change; the damage grew with the size of the swings.

The reason is that a loss requires a larger gain to undo it — down fifty needs up one hundred — so symmetric percentage moves are not symmetric in effect. Approximately, the compounded return sits below the average by about half the variance.

Where people get fooled: comparing strategies on average return. Two approaches with identical averages and different volatilities do not deliver the same result, and the smoother one wins without needing any better forecast. This is the arithmetic behind why volatility targeting improves outcomes while forecasting nothing — reducing the swings raises the compounded result on its own.
Variance drain.usage: Generally used to explain why a lower-volatility strategy can beat a higher-volatility one with the same average return.

Type I / Type II error.long:
A type I error is a false positive — concluding an effect exists when it does not. A type II error is a false negative — failing to detect one that is real. Every test that can be wrong can be wrong in both directions, and the two trade off against each other.

Tighten the threshold and fewer false discoveries get through, at the cost of missing more genuine ones. Loosen it and the reverse. There is no setting that reduces both, which makes the choice a judgement about which mistake is more expensive rather than a statistical question.

For a trader searching strategies, the costs are wildly asymmetric. A type II error means missing an edge — you keep your capital and remain where you were. A type I error means trading a strategy that does not work, sizing up as noise produces winning streaks, and discovering the truth through losses.

Where people get fooled: optimising to avoid the wrong error. Searching harder, loosening filters and testing more variants all reduce type II errors and inflate type I ones, which is the expensive direction. At a large enough trial count nearly every apparent discovery is a false positive, and the correct response is a higher bar, not a wider net.
Type I / Type II error.usage: Typically invoked when setting a significance threshold: which error you would rather make is a decision about costs, not a property of the data.

Cointegration.long:
Two price series are cointegrated when each wanders on its own but the distance between them stays bounded, so the spread tends to return toward a stable level. It is a stronger and more useful relationship than correlation.

The distinction matters. Correlation says two things tended to move in the same direction over some window, which can be true of series that drift apart permanently. Cointegration says the gap itself is anchored — that a widening carries a tendency to close. A spread trade needs the second property; the first is not sufficient and is where most pair selection goes wrong.

It is normally tested formally, with an Engle-Granger or Johansen procedure, and expressed as a hedge ratio saying how much of one instrument offsets the other.

Where people get fooled: cointegration is measured on history and can end without warning. The anchor is usually some economic link — the same inputs, the same customers, a shared index — and when that link breaks, the statistical relationship breaks with it while still testing positive on the trailing window. Screening thousands of pairs for the ones that historically co-moved also manufactures the appearance of it from noise, which is why a reason the two should be tied matters more than the test statistic.
Cointegration.usage: Generally the statistical basis for spread and pairs trading; correlation is not a substitute for it.

Half-life.long:
Half-life is the time a deviation from the mean takes to decay by half. Borrowed from physics, it puts a number on how quickly a mean-reverting series actually reverts, rather than leaving reversion as a vague expectation.

It is normally estimated by regressing the change in a spread against its level: the stronger the pull back toward the mean, the shorter the half-life. A spread with a three-day half-life is a different instrument from one with a sixty-day half-life, even if both are described as mean reverting.

The practical use is matching the holding period to the mechanism. Exiting a five-day half-life spread after one day means leaving before most of the expected reversion has occurred; holding a two-day spread for a month means sitting through the reversion and then whatever came after it.

Where people get fooled: treating the estimate as stable. Half-life is computed on a window and shifts with conditions — reversion that took days in a calm period can take weeks in a stressed one, or stop entirely if the relationship underneath has broken. A position sized for a quick round trip and held through a lengthening half-life is the standard way a mean-reversion book gets into trouble.
Half-life.usage: Typically estimated to set a holding period for a mean-reverting spread; it is a windowed estimate, not a constant.

Information ratio.long:
The information ratio divides excess return over a benchmark by the volatility of that excess — the tracking error. Where a Sharpe ratio measures return per unit of risk against cash, this measures it against whatever you are actually trying to beat.

That change of reference is the whole point. A strategy holding equities in a rising market posts a healthy Sharpe ratio simply by being invested; measured against the index it was supposed to beat, the same strategy may have added nothing at all. The information ratio isolates the part attributable to the active decisions.

It is the standard yardstick for anyone whose job is to beat a benchmark, and the honest one for a retail trader too, since the alternative to trading is usually holding an index rather than holding cash.

Where people get fooled: choosing a flattering benchmark. Against cash, or against a badly-chosen index, almost anything looks skilled — and the benchmark is picked by the person being measured, which is exactly the wrong incentive. The relevant comparison is the simplest thing you could have done instead with the same money and less effort, which for most people is buy and hold.
Information ratio.usage: Generally used to judge whether active decisions added anything beyond the benchmark; the benchmark choice decides the answer.

Fully diluted valuation.long:
Fully diluted valuation multiplies the current token price by the total supply that will ever exist, including everything still locked, vesting or unissued. Market capitalisation uses only the tokens circulating now.

The difference between the two figures is the part that matters. A token trading at a modest market cap can carry an FDV many times larger, and that gap represents supply scheduled to arrive later — held by teams, early investors and treasuries, most of it eventually saleable. Every unlock moves tokens from the locked column to the tradeable one at no cost to the holder.

Comparing projects on market cap alone therefore compares them on how much of their supply happens to be released so far, which is a scheduling decision rather than a measure of anything.

Where people get fooled: which number gets quoted depends on which is more flattering. Early on, a low float makes market cap look small and the token look cheap; the same project quoted on FDV looks expensive. Neither figure is dishonest on its own, and presenting only one is the technique. Read both together with the unlock schedule, and treat the gap as future supply with a calendar attached.
Fully diluted valuation.usage: Typically compared against market cap and the unlock schedule; the gap between them is supply that has not yet arrived.

Circulating supply.long:
Circulating supply is the number of tokens actually issued and freely tradeable — excluding those locked in vesting contracts, held by the treasury, or not yet minted. It is the denominator in market capitalisation.

Because market cap is price multiplied by this figure, the number directly controls how large or small a project appears. A token can be launched with a small fraction of its eventual supply circulating, which produces a modest market cap and a high price per token simultaneously — a combination that reads as early rather than as expensive.

There is also no single authority on the figure. Data aggregators apply their own rules about what counts as locked, and projects self-report, so the same token can show different supplies in different places.

Where people get fooled: treating it as a fixed property. It is a schedule, and the schedule is written by the issuer. A supply that grows steadily means a steady stream of new sellers regardless of what happens to demand, and comparing two projects' market caps without comparing what fraction of each supply is circulating compares almost nothing. The unlock calendar is the document that matters.
Circulating supply.usage: Generally the denominator in market cap; read it beside total supply and the unlock schedule rather than alone.

Liquidation price.long:
The liquidation price is the level at which a leveraged position's collateral no longer covers its losses and the venue force-closes it. It is calculated from the entry, the position size, the margin posted and the maintenance requirement, and every exchange displays it before the position is opened.

It is the single most consequential number on a leveraged position, because reaching it ends the trade regardless of what happens afterwards. A position liquidated at the bottom of a wick does not participate in the recovery two minutes later.

It moves. Adding margin pushes it further away, withdrawing brings it closer, and on cross-margin accounts it shifts as other positions gain or lose. Funding payments erode collateral over time, so a position held long enough drifts toward its own liquidation without the price moving at all.

Where people get fooled: treating it as the stop. A stop-loss is a level you chose; the liquidation price is the level at which you have already lost everything committed to that trade. Any sane position has a stop far in front of it — and on venues where liquidations cascade, the price can trade briefly through a cluster of them and recover, taking out everyone whose only protection was the exchange's own threshold.
Liquidation price.usage: Typically shown by the venue at order entry; it moves with margin, funding and other positions on cross margin.

Sandwich attack.long:
A sandwich attack places one transaction immediately before a victim's and another immediately after it. The first pushes the price against the victim, whose trade then executes at the worse level; the second closes the position into the move the victim's own order created.

It is possible because pending transactions are publicly visible before they are settled. A bot watching that queue can see a large order coming, calculate the price impact, and pay for a position ahead of it in the block. This is the most common form of MEV, and it applies specifically to trades on automated market makers, where price impact is a deterministic function of order size.

The defences are practical rather than clever: tighter slippage tolerance so an unfavourable fill reverts instead of executing, splitting large orders, using pools with more depth, or routing through a private mempool that does not broadcast the transaction publicly.

Where people get fooled: a wide slippage tolerance set to stop transactions failing. That setting is precisely the room the attack needs — it defines the worst fill you have pre-agreed to accept, and a bot can extract close to that entire allowance. The transaction succeeding is not evidence it went well.
Sandwich attack.usage: Generally mitigated with tight slippage tolerance, order splitting, deeper pools or private transaction routing.

Priority fee.long:
A priority fee is an additional payment attached to a transaction to have it included sooner when blockspace is contested. Blocks hold a limited number of transactions and are assembled by whoever is producing them, so the fee is a bid in an auction for position.

The consequence is that transaction cost is not a fixed price but a function of demand at that instant. In quiet conditions the fee is negligible. During a liquidation cascade, a popular mint or a sharp move, the same transaction can cost many multiples more — and it is competing against everyone else trying to act on the same information.

This produces a correlation that matters: the cost of acting rises precisely when acting is most urgent. Closing a position during a crash is the moment fees spike, and an underpriced transaction sits unconfirmed while the price keeps moving.

Where people get fooled: budgeting for average conditions. Backtests and cost models built on typical fees understate the cost of the trades that actually mattered, because those trades happened in exactly the conditions that made fees expensive. The fee you will pay in a crisis is the one worth planning around.
Priority fee.usage: Typically set per transaction to compete for inclusion; it rises with congestion, which is when execution matters most.

Maker / taker.long:
Maker and taker are the two sides of a fee schedule. An order that rests in the book and waits adds liquidity and pays the maker rate; an order that crosses the spread to execute immediately removes liquidity and pays the taker rate. The taker rate is higher, and on some venues the maker rate is a rebate.

The model exists because a venue needs resting orders to be worth trading on, so it pays for them out of what it charges the impatient side. That makes the fee schedule a direct statement of what the exchange values.

For anything with meaningful turnover the difference compounds into a first-order cost. A strategy that always crosses the spread pays the taker rate on every entry and every exit, and at a hundred round trips a month that is a fixed drag before any question of whether the signals work.

Where people get fooled: comparing venues on the headline rate. The relevant figure is the one for how you actually trade — a venue with an attractive maker rebate and a punishing taker fee is expensive for a strategy that needs immediate fills. Working out your own maker-to-taker mix and pricing the schedule against it is a short piece of arithmetic that changes which venue is cheapest.
Maker / taker.usage: Generally the largest controllable cost for a high-turnover strategy; price the schedule against your own fill mix.

Post-only order.long:
A post-only order will not execute against a resting order. If it would cross the spread on arrival, the venue cancels it rather than filling it, guaranteeing that when it does execute it is as a maker.

Its purpose is fee control. On a schedule where takers pay several times what makers pay — or where makers receive a rebate — the difference decides whether a high-turnover strategy is viable. Post-only removes the risk of an order accidentally crossing because the book moved in the instant between decision and arrival.

The cost is certainty of placement. An order that would have crossed simply does not exist, so a strategy using post-only has to handle rejections and decide whether to re-price, wait or abandon the attempt.

Where people get fooled: assuming the order is resting when it was rejected. A system that fires post-only orders and does not check the acknowledgement can believe it has a position it does not have — the exact class of error reconciliation exists to catch. It also fails most often in fast markets, where the book moves between decision and arrival, which is when the missing fill matters most.
Post-only order.usage: Typically used to stay on the maker fee tier; the trade-off is rejection rather than a worse fill.

NBBO.long:
The National Best Bid and Offer is the highest bid and lowest offer available across all US equity venues at a given moment, assembled into a single consolidated quote. US brokers have a duty to seek the best available terms for a customer order, and the NBBO is the reference that duty is measured against.

It exists because US equities trade on many venues at once. Without a consolidated view, the best price on one exchange would be invisible to someone looking at another, and the quote stitches those books into one number.

The reference is not the same as the outcome. Where an order actually executes depends on routing, and orders can fill at the NBBO, better than it through price improvement, or in a venue that does not display quotes at all.

Where people get fooled: treating the displayed quote as the depth available. The NBBO shows the best price and the size at that price, which may be a small fraction of what you are trying to trade — anything larger walks into worse levels immediately. It is also a snapshot that can be stale by the time an order arrives, which is the entire basis of the latency competition around it.
NBBO.usage: Generally the reference point for US best-execution obligations; it describes the top of the book, not the depth behind it.

Last look.long:
Last look is a practice, common in foreign exchange, where a liquidity provider may reject a trade after receiving it. The client sends an order against a quoted price and the provider has a brief window to accept or decline, having already seen the request.

The justification offered is protection against being picked off by faster participants on a stale quote. The effect is that a quoted price is an invitation rather than a commitment, and the option to withdraw sits with the party that published it.

The asymmetry is the substance of the objection. Rejections are not random: they cluster when the market has moved against the provider between quote and acceptance — which is when the client most wanted the fill. Regulators and industry codes have pushed for disclosure of hold times and rejection rates, and the practice has narrowed, but it persists.

Where people get fooled: judging a venue on its quoted spread. A tight spread that rejects when the market moves is worse than a wider one that always fills, and the difference does not appear in any spread comparison. Rejection rate and hold time are the figures that reveal it, and a provider unwilling to publish them has answered the question.
Last look.usage: Typically encountered in FX; evaluate a venue on rejection rate and hold time, not on the quoted spread alone.

Hidden order.long:
A hidden order rests at a venue without appearing in the displayed book. It can be filled by an incoming order but nobody sees it waiting. Iceberg orders are the partial version, showing a small slice while keeping the rest concealed.

The reason is impact. A large displayed order tells everyone what is coming, and the market moves away before it fills — so participants with size to work conceal it, accepting lower priority in exchange for not advertising their intention.

The consequence for anyone reading the book is that displayed depth understates real interest, and by an amount that varies by venue and moment. A level showing modest size can absorb far more than it appeared to.

Where people get fooled: order-flow reasoning built on the visible book. A thin level is not necessarily weak, a wall is not necessarily strong, and the difference between them is invisible by construction. This is the same limitation that applies to spoofing from the other direction — the displayed book overstates in one case and understates in the other, and neither is detectable in advance. What actually traded is the reliable record.
Hidden order.usage: Generally used to work size without signalling it; the practical effect is that displayed depth understates real interest.

Pre-mortem.long:
A pre-mortem inverts the post-mortem. Before committing, you assume the plan has already failed and write down the reasons, in the past tense, as though explaining what went wrong.

The technique comes from decision research, and the reason it works is that the framing removes the need to defend anything. Asked what might go wrong, people generate a short list of hedged concerns. Told it has already failed and asked why, they produce specifics — the assumption that was never checked, the scenario that was ignored, the dependency nobody owned.

Applied to trading, the output is concrete: this failed because the level was obvious and everyone was watching it; because the position was sized for a normal week and the release was scheduled; because there was no rule for what to do if it gapped through the stop.

Where people get fooled: doing it after entering. Once the position exists, every reason it might fail is also an argument that you have already made a mistake, and the mind supplies reassurance instead of analysis. The exercise only produces honest answers while nothing is at stake — which means before the trade, and preferably written down where it can be checked afterwards.
Pre-mortem.usage: Typically run before entry: assume the plan failed and write the reasons in the past tense, while nothing is committed.

Decision journal.long:
A decision journal records what you decided, what you expected, and why — written before the outcome is known. It is distinct from a trade log, which records what happened.

The purpose is to defeat hindsight. Memory does not store reasoning; it reconstructs it, and the reconstruction is shaped by how things turned out. A win is remembered as well judged and a loss as unlucky, which makes reviewing from memory a process that confirms whatever you already believe. A note written in advance cannot be edited by the result.

The useful fields are few: what you expected to happen, how confident you were, what would prove you wrong, and what you would do then. Reviewed in batches later, they show whether your confidence is calibrated — whether the trades you were sure about actually did better than the ones you were not.

Where people get fooled: writing it after the close. A journal entry composed once the result is known is a record of the explanation, not the decision, and it will look reasonable every time. The entry has to exist before the outcome or it is measuring nothing — which is the same reason a pre-registered prediction is worth more than a post-hoc one.
Decision journal.usage: Generally written before the outcome is known, recording the expectation and what would falsify it, then reviewed in batches.

Outside view.long:
The outside view judges a plan by what happened to everyone else who attempted something similar. The inside view judges it by the specifics of your own case — your preparation, your edge, your circumstances.

The research finding is that the outside view predicts better, and by a wide margin, on almost anything people forecast about themselves. Projects run long, budgets overrun, and ventures fail at rates their founders never predicted, because the inside view supplies detail while the outside view supplies the base rate, and the base rate is what actually governs.

In trading the outside view is the documented outcome for retail participants: most lose money over time, and the figure is published by regulators rather than inferred. That is the reference class you are joining.

Where people get fooled: the inside view always feels better informed, because it is. You genuinely do know more about your own situation than about the reference class — but the extra detail is mostly not predictive, while the base rate is. Every person in the losing majority also had specific reasons to think they were different, and those reasons felt exactly as compelling from the inside as yours do. Use the base rate as the starting estimate and require real evidence to move off it.
Outside view.usage: Generally used as the starting estimate: begin from what happened to the reference class, and move off it only with evidence.

Spread bet.long:
A spread bet is a leveraged position on price movement, priced per point of movement rather than as a quantity of an instrument. You never own the underlying; the provider is the counterparty, and the position is legally structured as a wager.

That structure is the entire reason the product exists. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, gains are generally free of capital gains tax and stamp duty because the activity is treated as betting rather than investing — which also means losses cannot be offset against gains elsewhere. The treatment depends on jurisdiction and personal circumstances, and it is a question for an accountant rather than a forum.

Mechanically it behaves like a CFD: leveraged, financed overnight, quoted with a spread that is the provider's revenue, and closed against the same provider that opened it.

Where people get fooled: the tax treatment doing the selling. A favourable rate on gains is worth nothing if the product's cost structure and leverage make gains unlikely — and the leverage available is precisely what makes the account short-lived for most users. Regulators publish the proportion of retail accounts losing money on these products; that figure, rather than the tax line, is the relevant number when deciding whether to use one.
Spread bet.usage: Typically used in the UK and Ireland for its tax treatment; mechanically it is a CFD with the provider as counterparty.

ETN.long:
An exchange-traded note is a debt obligation issued by a bank that promises the return of some index, minus fees. It trades on an exchange and tracks a benchmark, which makes it look like an ETF on a screen. It is not one.

The difference is what stands behind it. An ETF holds assets; if the sponsor fails, the holdings still exist and belong to the fund. An ETN holds nothing — it is an unsecured promise from the issuer, and its value depends on that institution remaining solvent. If the issuer fails, holders join the queue of creditors.

The structure exists because it can track things a fund cannot hold conveniently — some commodity and volatility exposures — and it removes tracking error, since the issuer simply owes the index return.

Where people get fooled: the screen presents it identically to an ETF, and the credit risk is invisible until it matters. Issuers can also suspend creation of new notes, at which point the price can detach from the index it supposedly tracks and trade at a large premium driven purely by supply. Volatility-linked notes in particular have been closed at short notice after sharp moves, at values far below what holders expected. Read what the thing actually is before treating it as a fund.
ETN.usage: Generally used for exposures a fund cannot hold easily; the return depends on the issuer's solvency, not on any pool of assets.
